title: Do Self-Improving Coding Agents Beat Textbook Baselines? Evidence from a Darwin Gödel Machine Port and Two Published Systems
why: Pre-registered audit of self-improving coding-agent harnesses (Darwin Gödel Machine + ADAS): compares retained scaffold edits from open-ended evolution loops against textbook harness moves (output-token limits, model-loop tweaks), one-shot redesigns, and placebo no-edit loops on LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench Verified—direct evidence on when harness RSI beats simple engineering baselines.
mechanism: Audit of harness-level open-ended evolution (DGM/ADAS retained scaffold/tool/instruction edits) vs textbook harness baselines and placebo loops; weights not the object of improvement
evaluation_signal: Author-reported pre-registered rounds: on hard LiveCodeBench with Claude Haiku 5.5, textbook move raising output-token limit to 16k recovers ~90% of best-loop agent gain at <half cost; on held-out SWE-bench Verified in DGM harness, released best DGM agent does not beat initial agent while three textbook moves on initial outperform best agent at ~1/4 cost
evidence_locator: mefyi abstract + plain-words summary; hexagonmath.org/2610.00598v1 title page; github README (paper DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23643512 / alt 23720889); first posted 25 Oct 2026

title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis
why: Non-weight multi-agent self-improvement: treats controller routing memory, specialist prompts, and procedural skills as scoped episodic memory; reflector assigns each failure to the owning scope and applies one guarded edit—beats ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS, and ADAS with fewer training executions.
mechanism: Structured episodic memory evolution for multi-agent systems: ownership-scoped updates to routing memory / specialist prompts / skills with backbone-independent guards (scoped, incremental, bounded)
evaluation_signal: Author-reported: KramaBench, AppWorld, BBEH; five backbones; four baselines ACE/GEPA/EvoMAS/ADAS; best overall on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over strongest baseline; 17–38% fewer training executions than most efficient baseline
